aflcio_description: The Senate muffed a chance to change its filibuster rule at the start of the 91st Congress. Shortly before he left office, Vice Pres. Humphrey ruled that only a majority vote was needed to act on a change in the Senate's rules at the start of a new Congress. If the Senate had sustained this ruling when it was appealed, the power of a minority to keep the majority from acting on legislation could have been curbed. But on Jan. 16, 1969, the Senate refused to sustain Humphrey's ruling by a 53-45 vote. For - right. Against - wrong.

Millions of poor Americans are ill-fed. A proposal by Sen. McGovern (D-S.D.) called for free food stamps for families with monthly incomes under $60 and authorized $1.25 billion for this program for fiscal 1970. The proposal was accepted 54-40, Sept. 24, 1969. For - right. Against - wrong.

Conservatives opposed to the war on poverty sought to give governors absolute veto power over legal services projects for the poor. A proposal by Sen. Murphy (R-Calif.) to this effect was approved 45-40, Oct. 14, 1969. For - wrong. Against - right. (Murphy's amendment was later knocked out of the final bill.)

Congressional conservatives have steadily chipped away at funding for the war on poverty, reducing the effectiveness of its programs. An amendment by Sen. Nelson (D-Wis.), adding $400 million to the amount the Appropriations Committee had recommended, was approved 60-32, Dec. 16, 1969. For - right. Against - wrong.

The House passed an amendment to prevent cutting federal funds to school districts refusing to desegregate. Despite Supreme Court decisions, the House plan said federal funds could not be denied school districts permitting so-called "freedom of choice" plans. Sen. Scott (R-Pa.) proposed an amendment to nullify the House action, and the Senate approved it, 52-37, Dec. 17, 1969. For - right. Against - wrong. (The House subsequently concurred. See House vote No. 9.)

aflcio_description: A consistent pattern of anti-union decisions, hostility to civil rights progress and gross insensitivity to conflicts of interest led the AFL-CIO and civil rights groups to oppose Pres. Nixon's nomination of Judge Clement F. Haynsworth, Jr., to the Supreme Court. On Nov. 21, 1969, the Senate rejected the nomination by a 55-45 vote. For - wrong. Against - right.

The $600 personal income tax exemption has been long outdated and is obviously inadequate. As a major measure of tax reform - one of the biggest issues in Congress and the nation - Sen. Gore (D-Tenn.) proposed increasing the personal exemption to $800. The Senate approved the Gore amendment 58-37, Dec. 3, 1969. For - right. Against - wrong. (The final bill changed this to a three-step increase to $750.)
